The Hypatian Chronicle's 1114 gloss on the Slavonic translation of John Malalas explicitly calls Dazhbog "son of Svarog" while equating Svarog with Hephaestus.

Svarozhich's own name is a patronymic/diminutive of Svarog ("son of" or "little Svarog"), but no medieval source directly links the East Slavic Svarog and the West Slavic Svarozhich cult at Riedegost; the connection is philological inference, not attested narrative.

No medieval text narrates a conflict between them. This edge represents Ivanov and Toporov's 1974 comparative reconstruction of a storm-god-versus-serpent combat, built from later folklore and place names, not an attested myth.
Sapling and Flint are twin grandsons of Sky Woman across every recorded Haudenosaunee telling used on this site, though tellers differ on the details of their birth and the outcome of their contest.
The Great Turtle offers to bear Sky Woman and the earth built up on his back, a direct alliance in the earth-diver episode recorded by Parker and Hewitt, not a family relationship.
Raven marries Fog Woman in the Tlingit story recorded by the Dauenhauers, before mistreating her and losing the salmon abundance she created.
Fog Woman is named as the daughter of Chief Fog-Over-the-Salmon in public retellings of the story.

In Swanton's telling, Raven transforms into a hemlock needle and is reborn as this old man's doted-on grandson, not his son; the site's relationship categories have no grandparent/grandchild type, so this edge is marked low confidence to flag that the actual kinship is one generation removed from what 'parent_of' literally states.
In the Sumerian myth Enlil and Ninlil, Nanna-Suen is the first child Ninlil conceives by Enlil.
Utu/Shamash, the sun, is regularly called the son of the moon god Nanna/Sin and his wife Ningal.
Many Sumerian texts make Inanna the daughter of Nanna and Ningal; others name An as her father.
In Afro-Brazilian Candomblé, Nanã is the mother of Omolu/Obaluaiê, the earth-and-smallpox orisha known in Yorubaland as Sopona.
Rigveda 10.17 says Saranyu bore the Ashvins and deserted 'both twinned pairs', the Ashvins and Yama with Yami.

Some scholars read Khors as another name or aspect of the sun god Dazhbog, since the Primary Chronicle lists them side by side; others see an Iranian moon or sun deity in his own right. No medieval source equates them.
A modern reconstruction (Ivanov and Toporov) pairs the thunder god with Mokosh as his wife; the Primary Chronicle lists both among Vladimir's idols but gives no marriage.
Hesiod's Theogony (371-374) names Helios, Selene, and Eos as the children of Hyperion and Theia.
Children of Hyperion and Theia (Theogony 371-374).
Children of Hyperion and Theia (Theogony 371-374).

Cronus and Tethys are both Titans, children of Gaia and Uranus.
The Homeric Hymn to Asclepius names him son of Apollo and Coronis.
Demeter bore Plutus to the hero Iasion in a thrice-plowed field in Crete (Theogony 969-974).
The Homeric Hymns call Castor and Polydeuces sons of Zeus and Leda; Pindar makes only Polydeuces Zeus's son, and the Odyssey names Tyndareus as father of both.
Kartikeya is born from Shiva's seed to destroy the demon Taraka.
Parvati is his mother in Puranic and devotional tradition, though many birth stories have him carried by Agni, Ganga, and the Krittikas rather than born from her.
Both are sons of Shiva and Parvati.
The Ramayana (Bala Kanda) makes Ganga the elder daughter of Himavat and Uma (Parvati) the younger.
In the Ramayana and Mahabharata versions of his birth, Ganga receives Shiva's fiery seed and bears the child.
Rigveda 4.30 praises Indra for smashing the wagon of Dawn, a rare hostile episode between them.
Skadi chose Njord by his feet as compensation for her father Thjazi; the marriage failed over mountains and sea (Gylfaginning 23).
Skadi fastens a venomous serpent above the bound Loki (Gylfaginning 50) and trades threats with him in Lokasenna.
Sun Wukong takes the Ruyi Jingu Bang from Ao Guang's palace and bullies the Dragon Kings for armor (Journey to the West, ch. 3).
The Dragon Kings serve as officials of the Jade Emperor's celestial court and petition him against Sun Wukong.
Enki and Ninhursag couple in Dilmun in the Sumerian myth that bears their names.
Sky and earth are paired in Akan prayer, the sky god named first and the earth second; many modern writers call Asase Yaa Nyame's wife, but no narrative marriage is recorded in the sources used here.
Tano is one of the two sons among whom Nyame divides the land in the Asante and Agni versions of the inheritance story.
Bia is Nyame's other son in the inheritance story, the brother who loses (or, in the Agni telling, wins) the fertile land.
Brothers and rivals, their quarrel over Nyame's land explains the courses of the two rivers.
Sky Woman is the wife of the Sky World's chief in the Seneca, Onondaga, and Mohawk tellings recorded by Parker and Hewitt.
Sky Woman gives birth to a daughter on the new earth in the recorded tellings.
The daughter of Sky Woman is the mother of the twins.
The daughter of Sky Woman is the mother of the twins and dies at Flint's birth.
In the Seneca cosmology Parker summarises, Sky Woman's daughter marries the gentle wind; other tellings recorded by Hewitt name the twins' father differently.
Parker describes the Thunderer as a servant of the good-minded twin, who assigns him his work of bringing rain and destroying underworld monsters.
Raven tricks Petrel out of his everlasting spring and escapes with the water (Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts, Sitka Raven cycle).
Raven attacks Old-woman-underneath until she agrees to let the tide rise and fall (Swanton, Sitka Raven cycle).

Attested pairing: in the treaties recorded in the Primary Chronicle (s.a. 907 and 971) the Rus' swear by Perun and by Volos, the cattle god, together. This is joint invocation in oaths, not a narrated alliance; the opposed 'enemy' reading of the same pair is a modern reconstruction.
Both are sons of Iapetus and Clymene (Hesiod, Theogony 507-514).
Night bore Nemesis without a partner (Hesiod, Theogony 223-224).
Night bore Death, with Sleep and Doom, without a partner (Hesiod, Theogony 211-212).
